turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Randomisation, Assignment, and Exposure.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The randomisation unit is assigned to a variant: user, account, household, clinician, clinic, region, or time period. Assignment should be probabilistic, persistent where needed, and independent between units.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Four units that teams often confuse
turns.text: What changes when we look at four units that teams often confuse?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The exposure unit encounters the treatment. A clinic may be assigned support but never activate it; a patient may belong to a treatment clinic before any updated data affects their referral.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The analysis unit is the level represented by observations in a metric: clinic, patient, referral, session, or event. Repeated events from one randomised unit are correlated. Treating them as independent creates overconfident uncertainty estimates.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The interference unit is the boundary within which one unit’s treatment can affect another’s outcome. Shared inventory, staff learning, network communication, and marketplace competition violate the simple assumption that one unit’s treatment does not influence others.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose randomisation at the same or a coarser level than important analysis and interference where feasible. Then use analysis that respects clustering and unequal exposure.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at assignment is not exposure?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Intention-to-treat analysis compares all assigned units and preserves randomisation. It estimates the effect of offering or assigning treatment, including non-use. This is often the most policy-relevant and trustworthy estimate.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Triggered analysis can improve sensitivity by focusing on units that could have been affected. But the trigger must be defined using conditions that do not depend differently on treatment. If treatment itself changes who reaches the trigger, conditioning can create selection bias. Log assignment and exposure separately and report trigger rates by variant.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Predefine eligibility, exclusions, persistence, identity, and cross-device behaviour. Post-hoc removal of inconvenient units breaks the comparison. Monitor sample-ratio mismatch, invariant pre-treatment characteristics, exposure parity, and variant switching before reading outcomes.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: a marketplace?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Randomising buyers to a recommendation can change which sellers receive demand, affecting control buyers through shared inventory. User-level assignment does not isolate effects. A market-level, geographic, switchback, or other clustered design may be needed, each with power and temporal assumptions. The unit is a property of the causal system, not a platform default.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Assignment–exposure collapse: assigned people are assumed to have experienced treatment. Event independence: thousands of clicks from a few clinics are treated as thousands of independent units. Treatment-dependent trigger: analysis conditions on behaviour caused by the variant. Identity leakage: devices or accounts switch arms.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Shared-resource interference: treatment consumes capacity available to control. Post-hoc eligibility: units are removed after outcomes are known.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Choose the randomisation unit from the service topology
turns.text: What changes when we look at choose the randomisation unit from the service topology?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Eligibility is determined before assignment. The system records assignment independently from exposure, repeated exposure, crossover, and outcome. Intention-to-treat estimates the effect of offering the variant under real compliance.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Per-protocol or treatment-on-treated analyses answer different questions and require stronger assumptions; they do not replace the primary design because the result looks larger.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Ethics limits experimentation. The team does not randomise a known accessibility fix or hide material transfer consequences. Uncertain safe alternatives can be tested with clinical and service guardrails, monitoring, and stop rules. The experiment report states the treatment, population, estimand, analysis, deviations, and interference.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: call-centre script?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Randomising customers fails if agents switch between scripts and carry learning across calls. Agent or shift clusters may be stronger, but scheduling, case mix, and small cluster count become part of the design.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Unit choice determines what causal claim is possible and who bears experimental risk. Senior practitioners involve data science, engineering, operations, privacy, and domain owners before feature implementation, because randomisation is often baked into architecture.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: They resist increased statistical power when it requires a unit that violates service reality or exposes people unsafely.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Protect the comparison from assignment to analysis
turns.text: What changes when we look at protect the comparison from assignment to analysis?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Randomising individuals may create interference when staff serve both variants or learn a new workflow. Cluster or time-based designs have different power and confounding risks. Sample-ratio mismatch, missing exposure, and unequal latency are investigated before interpreting effect. The assignment design follows the causal question and service topology.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a checkout experiment. Customers are assigned to a new delivery-date display, but some never reach the screen. Analyse assignment separately from actual exposure and check that allocation, eligibility, and event logging worked as planned. Otherwise the apparent lift may reflect who saw the change rather than what the change did.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Take a published experiment. Ask whether assignment occurred by user, session, device, organisation, or geography; whether outcomes share resources; and whether “users who saw” is a randomised or selected group.
